title: Senegal reinstated as 2025 AFCON champion after winning appeal | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Senegal has been reinstated as the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) men’s champion after winning an appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

It follows 10 months of uncertainty after one of the most chaotic andcontroversialfinals in soccer history.

Senegal won the final back in January, but beaten finalist Morocco was awarded the title two months later after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) appeal board deemed Senegal had “forfeited the final” after temporarily walking off the pitch in protest.

Now, though, things are back to where they started.

The game will be remembered most for the decision by some of Senegal’s players to walk off the pitch in protest of a penalty being awarded to Morocco in the final moments of regulation time, with the score at 0-0.

The referee’s decision came just minutes after Senegal had a goal controversially disallowed at the other end, and it all contributed to an implosion on the pitch and in the stands.

Senegal’s head coach Pape Thiaw ordered his players off the field as a way of protest. Some of his team listened while a handful of others stayed on the field to try calm the situation.

After a lengthy stoppage of play, all of Senegal’s players returned to the pitch, only to watch Morocco’s Brahim Díaz miss the controversial penalty.

Senegal then scored a brilliant goal in extra time to win 1-0 and become AFCON champions for a second time.

The reaction from the Senegal team was in part the product of a deep-rooted mistrust in African soccer, notably between the national federations and CAF.

Frustrated by the manner of defeat, the Moroccan soccer federation (FRMF) launched an appeal. CAF then overturned the result and awarded Morocco a 3-0 win by default.

In explaining the decision, the governing bodycitedArticle 82 of tournament’s regulations, which states: “If, for any reason whatsoever, a team withdraws from the competition or does not report for a match, or refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition.”

The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) then appealed that verdict. In a statement on Tuesday, CAS said its decision to reinstate Senegal as champion was “unanimous.”

We’re living in a strange world if soccer matches are now being decided in the courtroom.

It’s been over 300 days since Senegal lifted that trophy on the pitch in Rabat and the fact we’ve only now gotten a conclusion is an embarrassing indictment of the sport.

The final itself was already a disappointing note on which to end what was a brilliant tournament, and the fallout only amplified how poorly this has all been handled by those running African soccer.

But you have to feel for both sets of players. For the Senegalese team, they saw their dreams come true before they were seemingly snatched away two months later by suits in a boardroom.

Then you have the Moroccan players who have tasted defeat both on the pitch and now again almost a year later.

For many, though, honoring what the scoreboard said at full time was always the right thing to do. Ultimately, Morocco agreed to continue the game and wouldn’t have had complaints had they scored that last-minute penalty in the final.

But while we’ve avoided setting a worrying precedent for soccer – in overturning results after the case – the bitter taste from this controversy will linger around African soccer for quite some time.
